tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

complexity.reasoning: Migrated from legacy per-task YAML (no AI re-assessment).

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

complexity.reasoning: Migrated from legacy per-task YAML (no AI re-assessment).

tasks.title: Implement Cursor Smoothing Algorithm
tasks.description:
Transform shaky/jerky cursor motion into smooth curves.

Requirements:
- Implement Catmull-Rom or similar spline interpolation
- Configurable smoothing intensity (None, Light, Medium, Heavy)
- Real-time preview of smoothed path
- Preserve key events (clicks) at precise locations

Technical approach:
- Apply spline interpolation between cursor waypoints
- Maintain click event accuracy while smoothing movement
- Implement adjustable tension parameter
- Generate smoothed cursor frame overlay

Deliverables:
- Smoothing algorithm module
- Configurable intensity slider
- Preview rendering
- Performance benchmark (should handle 60fps)

tasks.title: Implement Automatic Cursor Zoom
tasks.description:
Detect cursor actions and automatically zoom the viewport.

Requirements:
- Detect "interesting" cursor actions (clicks, drags, pauses)
- Calculate appropriate zoom level and pan
- Smooth zoom transitions (ease-in/out)
- Timeline-based zoom editing UI

Technical approach:
- Analyze cursor velocity and events
- Apply heuristics to determine zoom-worthy moments
- Implement smooth camera pan/zoom transforms
- Store zoom keyframes in timeline

Deliverables:
- Zoom detection algorithm
- Smooth zoom animation system
- Timeline zoom controls
- Auto vs manual zoom modes

tasks.description:
Implement cursor appearance and behavior controls.

Features:

- High-resolution cursor replacement when size increased
- Auto-hide static cursor after configurable timeout
- Loop cursor position for seamless looping videos
- Custom cursor image support

- Implement fade-out animation for auto-hide
- Calculate return path for loop position

- Size slider with presets
- Auto-hide toggle and timeout
- Loop position option

tasks.title: Implement Audio Recording
tasks.description:
Add microphone and system audio capture.

Features:
- Microphone recording
- System audio capture (all apps or selected)
- Background noise reduction
- Audio normalization
- Volume level meters
- Separate audio track control

Technical approach:
- Use WASAPI for capture: microphone via the default input endpoint, system audio via WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint (Windows 10+ supports loopback capture cleanly; per-process capture needs an audio-graph/IAudioCaptureClient approach or process injection and is harder)
- Implement noise gate filter and (optional) AEC/voice processing via Media Foundation Voice Capture DSP (MFPKEY_WMAAFCMA_FORMAT; the Voice Capture DSP provides acoustic-echo cancellation, noise suppression, AGC)
- Apply compression/normalization (DSP / manual)
- Sync audio with video timeline using shared high-resolution timestamps

Deliverables:
- Audio capture module
- Noise reduction filter
- Audio level meters
- Export with mixed audio

tasks.title: Implement Aspect Ratio Modes
tasks.description:
Support horizontal and vertical output modes.

Features:
- Horizontal mode (16:9 landscape)
- Vertical mode (9:16 portrait for social media)
- One-click mode switching
- Auto-adjust all zooms when switching modes
- Social media presets (TikTok, IG Reels, YouTube Shorts)

Technical approach:
- Store zoom keyframes as relative positions
- Recalculate transforms on aspect ratio change
- Maintain content focus area
- Add padding/cropping as needed

Deliverables:
- Aspect ratio selector
- Auto-zoom recalculation
- Preview in both modes
- Social media presets

tasks.title: RecordingOverlay + system tray
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.1 + Phase U1. The daily-driver floating control: target selector
(FullScreen/Display/Window/Region → CaptureOptions.Target), mic + system-audio toggles
(→ CaptureOptions.Capture*), Start/Pause/Stop (→ RecordingSession.*), live REC indicator + timer
(→ RecordingSession.State / RecordedDurationMs). System tray icon entry point (New/Recent/Settings/Quit).
Build RecordingViewModel (INPC) wrapping RecordingSession — the engine exposes only polling State
today (ui-prd §9.2 gap), so the VM must surface state-change. Always-on-top acrylic pill.
Permission handling: inline message + Windows-Settings deep-link when mic/screen-capture denied.
Bindings: CaptureOptions, RecordingSession, IScreenCapture, CursorEventLogger.
tasks.details: RecordingViewModel.cs; RecordingOverlay.xaml; tray icon; region click-drag picker.
tasks.testStrategy: VM state transitions unit-tested; overlay launches, records raw via UI, stops cleanly.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from ui-prd.md phasing.

tasks.title: PostRecordWindow + ExportSheet (auto effects)
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.2 + §6.4 + Phase U2. The value-reveal window: large preview rendering
auto-applied zoom + smoothed cursor (FrameCompositor.Compose → SoftwareBitmapSource for v1), with
the Export button + collapsed-by-default "Edit zoom" toggle. ExportSheet as ContentDialog over it:
preset chips (→ ExportSettingsViewModel.Presets), Custom expand, validation bound to
ValidationError/CanExport, output-path picker, progress bar (→ ExportPipeline.RunAsync IAsyncEnumerable
<ExportProgress>) + Cancel (CancellationToken). Uses the existing ExportSettingsViewModel as-is.
This delivers the happy path: record → polished MP4 via UI, auto effects only (no manual timeline).
tasks.details: PostRecordWindow.xaml; ExportSheet.xaml; preview seeks to ~25% to show a zoom immediately.
tasks.testStrategy: End-to-end via UI: record → stop → preview shows zoom → export → valid MP4 on disk.

tasks.title: Style panel + aspect switcher + live preview

with SizePresets detents, auto-hide toggle+timeout, loop, custom-image picker), Background tab
(background color/image, padding, device frame — engine gap ui-prd §9.4, can shell controls with

tasks.testStrategy: VM two-way binding unit-tested; each tweak shows instant preview feedback.

tasks.title: TimelinePanel (power-user keyframe editor)
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.3 + Phase U4. Collapsed until "Edit zoom" toggled; slides in below preview.
Canvas-based track (WinUI has no built-in timeline control): time ruler + video track + zoom-keyframe
track (→ RecordingTimeline.Segments + ZoomProgram.Keyframes). Interactions: drag keyframe in time
(→ ZoomProgram.ReplaceAt + SnapToKeyframe), drag focus/scale, trim handles (→ TrimEdges), razor/cut
(→ Cut), scrub playhead (→ SetPlayhead; preview seeks). Build TimelineViewModel (INPC, observable
keyframe/segment collections — ui-prd §8). Keep genuinely light — NOT Camtasia's multi-track editor.
tasks.details: TimelineViewModel.cs; TimelinePanel.xaml; custom Canvas track + draggable keyframe thumbs.
tasks.testStrategy: VM commands unit-tested; drag a keyframe, trim, cut — durations update correctly.

tasks.title: SettingsWindow + persistence layer
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.5 + Phase U5 + resolves ui-prd §9.1 (persistence) and §9.3 (device
enumeration). App-level defaults that persist across sessions (JSON file or ApplicationData
.LocalSettings): default smoothing/zoom/codec, hotkey map, mic device. Standard SettingsPage with
SettingsCard controls (Fluent). Add the persistence layer the engine lacks (ExportSettings,
CursorCustomization, ZoomDetectionOptions are in-memory only). Add window/monitor + mic device
enumeration surfaces for the target/mic pickers (FfmpegAudioCapture.ListMicrophones exists for mics;
WGC/WASAPI path has none — ui-prd §9.3).
tasks.details: SettingsService (JSON persist); DeviceEnumeration surface; SettingsWindow.xaml.
tasks.testStrategy: Settings round-trip (set → restart → values restored); device list populates.

tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.title: Implement Cursor Smoothing Algorithm
tasks.description:
Transform shaky/jerky cursor motion into smooth curves.

Requirements:
- Implement Catmull-Rom or similar spline interpolation
- Configurable smoothing intensity (None, Light, Medium, Heavy)
- Real-time preview of smoothed path
- Preserve key events (clicks) at precise locations

Technical approach:
- Apply spline interpolation between cursor waypoints
- Maintain click event accuracy while smoothing movement
- Implement adjustable tension parameter
- Generate smoothed cursor frame overlay

Deliverables:
- Smoothing algorithm module
- Configurable intensity slider
- Preview rendering
- Performance benchmark (should handle 60fps)

tasks.title: Implement Automatic Cursor Zoom
tasks.description:

- Implement smooth camera pan/zoom transforms
- Store zoom keyframes in timeline

Deliverables:

- Smooth zoom animation system
- Timeline zoom controls
- Auto vs manual zoom modes

tasks.title: Implement Audio Recording
tasks.description:
Add microphone and system audio capture.

Features:
- Microphone recording
- System audio capture (all apps or selected)
- Background noise reduction
- Audio normalization
- Volume level meters
- Separate audio track control

Technical approach:
- Use WASAPI for capture: microphone via the default input endpoint, system audio via WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint (Windows 10+ supports loopback capture cleanly; per-process capture needs an audio-graph/IAudioCaptureClient approach or process injection and is harder)
- Implement noise gate filter and (optional) AEC/voice processing via Media Foundation Voice Capture DSP (MFPKEY_WMAAFCMA_FORMAT; the Voice Capture DSP provides acoustic-echo cancellation, noise suppression, AGC)
- Apply compression/normalization (DSP / manual)
- Sync audio with video timeline using shared high-resolution timestamps

Deliverables:
- Audio capture module
- Noise reduction filter
- Audio level meters
- Export with mixed audio

tasks.title: Implement Aspect Ratio Modes
tasks.description:

- Vertical mode (9:16 portrait for social media)
- One-click mode switching
- Auto-adjust all zooms when switching modes
- Social media presets (TikTok, IG Reels, YouTube Shorts)

Technical approach:
- Store zoom keyframes as relative positions
- Recalculate transforms on aspect ratio change
- Maintain content focus area
- Add padding/cropping as needed

Deliverables:
- Aspect ratio selector
- Auto-zoom recalculation
- Preview in both modes
- Social media presets

tasks.title: RecordingOverlay + system tray
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.1 + Phase U1. The daily-driver floating control: target selector
(FullScreen/Display/Window/Region → CaptureOptions.Target), mic + system-audio toggles
(→ CaptureOptions.Capture*), Start/Pause/Stop (→ RecordingSession.*), live REC indicator + timer
(→ RecordingSession.State / RecordedDurationMs). System tray icon entry point (New/Recent/Settings/Quit).
Build RecordingViewModel (INPC) wrapping RecordingSession — the engine exposes only polling State
today (ui-prd §9.2 gap), so the VM must surface state-change. Always-on-top acrylic pill.
Permission handling: inline message + Windows-Settings deep-link when mic/screen-capture denied.
Bindings: CaptureOptions, RecordingSession, IScreenCapture, CursorEventLogger.
tasks.details: RecordingViewModel.cs; RecordingOverlay.xaml; tray icon; region click-drag picker.
tasks.testStrategy: VM state transitions unit-tested; overlay launches, records raw via UI, stops cleanly.

tasks.title: PostRecordWindow + ExportSheet (auto effects)
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.2 + §6.4 + Phase U2. The value-reveal window: large preview rendering
auto-applied zoom + smoothed cursor (FrameCompositor.Compose → SoftwareBitmapSource for v1), with
the Export button + collapsed-by-default "Edit zoom" toggle. ExportSheet as ContentDialog over it:
preset chips (→ ExportSettingsViewModel.Presets), Custom expand, validation bound to
ValidationError/CanExport, output-path picker, progress bar (→ ExportPipeline.RunAsync IAsyncEnumerable
<ExportProgress>) + Cancel (CancellationToken). Uses the existing ExportSettingsViewModel as-is.
This delivers the happy path: record → polished MP4 via UI, auto effects only (no manual timeline).
tasks.details: PostRecordWindow.xaml; ExportSheet.xaml; preview seeks to ~25% to show a zoom immediately.
tasks.testStrategy: End-to-end via UI: record → stop → preview shows zoom → export → valid MP4 on disk.

tasks.title: Style panel + aspect switcher + live preview
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.2 Style tabs + Phase U3. Cursor tab (→ CursorCustomization: size slider
with SizePresets detents, auto-hide toggle+timeout, loop, custom-image picker), Background tab
(background color/image, padding, device frame — engine gap ui-prd §9.4, can shell controls with

tasks.details: CursorSettingsViewModel.cs; ZoomSettingsViewModel.cs; StylePanel.xaml tabs.
tasks.testStrategy: VM two-way binding unit-tested; each tweak shows instant preview feedback.

tasks.title: TimelinePanel (power-user keyframe editor)
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.3 + Phase U4. Collapsed until "Edit zoom" toggled; slides in below preview.
Canvas-based track (WinUI has no built-in timeline control): time ruler + video track + zoom-keyframe
track (→ RecordingTimeline.Segments + ZoomProgram.Keyframes). Interactions: drag keyframe in time
(→ ZoomProgram.ReplaceAt + SnapToKeyframe), drag focus/scale, trim handles (→ TrimEdges), razor/cut
(→ Cut), scrub playhead (→ SetPlayhead; preview seeks). Build TimelineViewModel (INPC, observable
keyframe/segment collections — ui-prd §8). Keep genuinely light — NOT Camtasia's multi-track editor.
tasks.details: TimelineViewModel.cs; TimelinePanel.xaml; custom Canvas track + draggable keyframe thumbs.
tasks.testStrategy: VM commands unit-tested; drag a keyframe, trim, cut — durations update correctly.

tasks.title: SettingsWindow + persistence layer
tasks.description:
UI PRD §6.5 + Phase U5 + resolves ui-prd §9.1 (persistence) and §9.3 (device
enumeration). App-level defaults that persist across sessions (JSON file or ApplicationData
.LocalSettings): default smoothing/zoom/codec, hotkey map, mic device. Standard SettingsPage with
SettingsCard controls (Fluent). Add the persistence layer the engine lacks (ExportSettings,
CursorCustomization, ZoomDetectionOptions are in-memory only). Add window/monitor + mic device
enumeration surfaces for the target/mic pickers (FfmpegAudioCapture.ListMicrophones exists for mics;
WGC/WASAPI path has none — ui-prd §9.3).
tasks.details: SettingsService (JSON persist); DeviceEnumeration surface; SettingsWindow.xaml.
tasks.testStrategy: Settings round-trip (set → restart → values restored); device list populates.

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.description:

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

- Background noise reduction
- Audio normalization

- Separate audio track control

Technical approach:
- Use WASAPI for capture: microphone via the default input endpoint, system audio via WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint (Windows 10+ supports loopback capture cleanly; per-process capture needs an audio-graph/IAudioCaptureClient approach or process injection and is harder)

Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.title: Implement Audio Recording

- Microphone recording
- System audio capture (all apps or selected)
- Background noise reduction
- Audio normalization
- Volume level meters
- Separate audio track control

Technical approach:
- Use WASAPI for capture: microphone via the default input endpoint, system audio via WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint (Windows 10+ supports loopback capture cleanly; per-process capture needs an audio-graph/IAudioCaptureClient approach or process injection and is harder)

- Sync audio with video timeline using shared high-resolution timestamps

- Audio level meters

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

tasks.title: Define Technical Architecture
tasks.description:
DECISION RECORD — Tech stack & architecture (RESOLVED).

Chosen stack: C# / .NET 8 + WinUI 3 (native Windows 11).
Rationale: first-class access to the Windows media APIs that are essential to
this product's core differentiator (polished effects while capturing at 60fps
with a responsive UI), lowest runtime overhead, and fully buildable/runnable on
the Windows dev machine. macOS/Linux support is out of scope for v1.

Options evaluated:
- C# / .NET + WinUI 3 (CHOSEN) — native WGC/Media Foundation/WASAPI, best perf.
- Tauri + React — React UI is great for the timeline, but capture/encode would
  require bridging to Windows APIs via `windows-rs` (added complexity).
- Electron + React — largest ecosystem, but Chromium overhead works against the
  "responsive during recording" success metric.
- Flutter — weakest native-media story on Windows (needs platform channels).

Windows 11 native API mapping (source of truth for engine tasks):
- Screen capture 60fps, low overhead → Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API,
  frames delivered as Direct3D 11 textures to a DirectX/Direct2D swap chain.
- Hardware video encode → Media Foundation (NVENC / Intel QSV / AMD AMF).
- System audio capture → WASAPI loopback on the render endpoint.
- Microphone capture → WASAPI capture endpoint (+ Voice Capture DSP for AEC /
  noise suppression / AGC where needed).
- High-precision cursor tracking → WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook and/or
  GetCursorInfo polling, timestamped with QueryPerformanceCounter.

Layered architecture (top → bottom):
- UI Layer (WinUI 3): recording UI, timeline editor, preview, export dialog.
- Recording Engine: WGC capture, cursor tracker, WASAPI audio.
- Processing Pipeline: zoom detection, Catmull-Rom cursor smoothing, effects
  render (GPU/Direct2D compositing).
- Export Engine: Media Foundation encode, MP4 (H.264) mux, format/aspect-ratio
  options, progress + cancellation.

Out of scope for v1: macOS, Linux, iOS-device-recording USB capture, cloud sync.

tasks.title: Implement Screen Recording Engine
tasks.description:
Build the core recording functionality:
- Full screen or selected area recording
- High-quality capture (60fps target)
- Low CPU overhead during recording
- Cursor position and click event tracking (high precision)
- Raw frame buffer storage for processing

Technical considerations:
- Use Windows-native APIs: Windows Graphics Capture (WGC) API for GPU-accelerated screen/monitor/window/region capture at 60fps; render captured frames to a Direct3D 11 texture (DirectX surface) for downstream compositing
- Track cursor via WH_MOUSE_LL low-level mouse hook (and/or GetCursorInfo + per-frame cursor capture from WGC, which can include the system cursor in the frame) — log position + click events with high-resolution timestamps (QueryPerformanceCounter)
- Implement efficient frame buffering (pool of D3D11 textures / staging buffers; avoid GPU→CPU readback on the hot path)
- Log cursor events with timestamps for later processing
- Consider memory footprint for long recordings (stream to disk / chunked buffers rather than holding all raw frames)

Deliverables:
- Working screen capture module (WGC-based)
- Cursor event logger
- Basic recording controls (start/stop/pause)
- Raw output verification

enumeration). App-level defaults that persist across sessions (JSON file or ApplicationData
.LocalSettings): default smoothing/zoom/codec, hotkey map, mic device. Standard SettingsPage with
SettingsCard controls (Fluent). Add the persistence layer the engine lacks (ExportSettings,
CursorCustomization, ZoomDetectionOptions are in-memory only). Add window/monitor + mic device
enumeration surfaces for the target/mic pickers (FfmpegAudioCapture.ListMicrophones exists for mics;
WGC/WASAPI path has none — ui-prd §9.3).
tasks.details: SettingsService (JSON persist); DeviceEnumeration surface; SettingsWindow.xaml.
tasks.testStrategy: Settings round-trip (set → restart → values restored); device list populates.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from ui-prd.md phasing.

tasks.title: Webcam overlay (PiP) capture + render
tasks.description:
PRD P1 #3 — Webcam Recording. Overlay the webcam on the recording as a
    picture-in-picture; auto-zoom-out (shrink PiP) when the cursor is active so it doesn't
    occlude content. Engine: add a webcam capture module (MediaFoundation MediaCapture or
    ffmpeg dshow video input) producing frames; FrameCompositor renders the PiP inset.
    UI: a webcam toggle in the RecordingOverlay + a draggable PiP in PostRecordWindow's preview.
    Deliverables: webcam capture module, PiP compositing in FrameCompositor, webcam UI toggle.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from PRD P1/P2 + UI polish items.

tasks.title: Visual customization: backgrounds, padding, shadows, borders
tasks.description:
PRD P1 #5 — Visual Customization. Background color/image behind the recording,
    outer spacing/padding, drop shadows, inset/border effects. Engine: extend FrameCompositor
    to render a background layer + padding frame + shadow + border around the captured content
    (the aspect-framing math exists in AspectRatioConverter; this adds the visual render).
    UI: complete the Background tab in StylePanel (controls exist but render was deferred —
    ui-prd §9.4 gap). Deliverables: background/padding/shadow/border render in FrameCompositor,
    Background tab wired in StylePanel.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from PRD P1/P2 + UI polish items.

tasks.title: Motion blur on cursor movement
tasks.description:
PRD P2 #1 — Motion Blur. Natural motion blur trailing the cursor based on its
    velocity; configurable intensity. Engine: in the CursorSmoother/FrameCompositor path,
    sample recent cursor positions and render a fading trail (alpha-blended ghost cursors)
    proportional to speed. UI: a motion-blur intensity slider in the Cursor tab of StylePanel.
    Deliverables: motion-blur render pass, intensity control.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from PRD P1/P2 + UI polish items.

tasks.title: Keyboard shortcut display (keycap overlay)
tasks.description:
PRD P2 #2 — Keyboard Shortcut Display. Detect pressed keys (Win32
    GetAsyncKeyState / WH_KEYBOARD_LL hook) and render stylish keycap visualizations in the
    recording. Position customization. Engine: a KeyboardHook + key-event logger (parallel to
    CursorHook); FrameCompositor renders keycap glyphs. UI: a shortcuts-display toggle +
    position picker. Deliverables: keyboard hook + logger, keycap render, display controls.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from PRD P1/P2 + UI polish items.

tasks.title: Advanced export: GIF, WebM, presets
tasks.description:
PRD P2 #4 — Advanced Export. GIF export, WebM export, custom bitrate/quality
    settings, export presets (social media, web). Engine: extend the encoder layer — FfmpegEncoder
    already supports codec switching; add GIF (palettegen + paletteuse) and WebM (VP9) muxing,
    plus named social presets. UI: add GIF/WebM to the ExportSheet codec selector + a preset
    dropdown. Deliverables: GIF + WebM encode paths, social export presets, UI options.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from PRD P1/P2 + UI polish items.

tasks.title: Polish: tray context menu + window enumeration wiring
tasks.description:
UI polish items flagged at the end of the UI build. (1) TrayController: add the
    right-click context menu (New Recording / Recent / Settings / Quit) — the icon + activate
    work today but the menu is missing. (2) Wire WindowEnumeration.ListWindows() into the
    RecordingOverlay's target ComboBox so the "Window" option populates real on-screen windows
    (currently static labels). Deliverables: tray context menu, dynamic window-target picker.

complexity.reasoning: Derived from PRD P1/P2 + UI polish items.

tasks.title: Runtime smoke test: launch app, validate GUI flow
tasks.description:
Launch ScreenStudio.App.exe in a real desktop session and validate the full GUI
    flow: window renders, RecordingOverlay works, record→stop→PostRecordWindow opens, preview
    shows auto-zoom, export produces a real MP4. Everything compiles + unit/E2E tests pass, but
    the GUI itself has never been runtime-validated in a display session. Deliverable: a manual
    or automated smoke-test pass confirming the app runs end-to-end on the desktop.
